title: Refer it back
hookLine: in a dispute, refer it to Allah and the messenger (4:59)
carry: make it about what, not who

cards: Two siblings are arguing about how to care for an aging parent. One wants to move her in; one wants a care home. It's been weeks, and each conversation ends in the same place, louder.
Neither is wrong to care. The trouble is they keep arguing about who's right, instead of asking what they both already agree should decide it.
The verse right after yesterday's gives a method for exactly that kind of stuck.

teach.h: OBEY, OBEY, AND THOSE IN AUTHORITY
teach.b: Verse 59 opens: O you who believe, obey God, and obey the messenger, and those in authority among you. Then, in Pickthall's words: "and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger."
That, the verse says, is better, and more fitting in the end. Look at the grammar. Obey is said before God, and again before the messenger, but not before those in authority, ulu al-amr.
Some commentators drew a lesson from that: obedience to people in charge is tied to obedience to God, not free-standing. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it vivid.
A commander, angry with his troops, ordered them to build a fire and walk into it.

teach.h: THE FIRE THEY REFUSED TO ENTER
teach.b: They refused. When the Prophet ﷺ heard, he said if they had entered it they would never have come out; obedience is only in what is right. Who are those in authority?
Sunni scholars give different answers: rulers and commanders, or the learned, or both. Shia Muslims understand them as the Imams of the Prophet's family.

And after the Prophet's death, refer it to God and the messenger is commonly read as: to the Qur'an and to his Sunnah, his example. So the verse doesn't say the loudest wins, or whoever's in charge wins.
When you disagree, step back from the two of you and take the question to a source you both already accept.
For the siblings, that might be the Qur'an's command to honor parents, or simply what their mother herself wants.

teach.h: REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.
teach.b: Disputes stay stuck when they're about who. They move when they're about what.

how: Muslims resolve questions of religious practice by referring them to the Qur'an and the Sunnah, through scholars and the schools of law; 4:59 is a foundation of Islamic legal reasoning and of the principle that obedience to authority is limited to what is right.

o: the angels who carry out God's command

games.q: refer it back — tap the pairs.

s: 4:59 says whoever is in charge always gets the final word
disputes are referred to God and the messenger, and obedience is only in what is right.
the word obey is not repeated before those in authority
commentators read this as making their authority dependent, not free-standing.
scholars agree on exactly who those in authority are
some say rulers, some say the learned, some say both.

games.q: your commander, angry, orders you and your troops to light a fire and walk into it. what did the troops in the hadith do?
o: they obeyed; he was in authority.
they refused, and the Prophet said obedience is only in what is right.
they ran away and left the army.
games.why: they refused, and the Prophet said had they entered they would never have come out (Sahih al-Bukhari).

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in, and take the names out of it: say the question itself in one plain sentence.
Then ask what you'd both accept as the judge, a text you both honor, a rule you both signed, what the person most affected actually wants, and picture taking the question to it together.

wordCard.voice: Ulu al-amr, those in authority. Obedience to them is tied to obedience to God, not free-standing, from 4:59.

orig.note: Arabic: then refer it back to God and the messenger (4:59); rudd means to return, to send back.

carryVoice: Your line: make it about what, not who. A shared source can settle what two loud voices can't. Day three hundred eighty-three, done.

sources.q: and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7145 (the commander and the fire)
